title: Bipolar vs. Depression: How to Tell the Difference
description: Bipolar disorder is often misdiagnosed as depression. Warning signs, key differences, why correct diagnosis matters, and what to discuss with your doctor.

content.text: It takes an average of 8 years to correctly diagnose bipolar disorder. Most people are first diagnosed with depression. Here's why it matters and how to tell the difference.

items: People seek help during depression, not mania
Mania feels good (at first), so it's not reported as a problem
Hypomania (mild mania) is easily missed
Depression symptoms look identical
Some bipolar patients have more depression than mania

content.text: Warning Signs You Might Have Bipolar, Not Just Depression

items: Periods of unusually elevated mood or energy
Decreased need for sleep (feeling rested on 3-4 hours)
Racing thoughts, rapid speech
Taking on many projects simultaneously
Impulsive spending, risky behavior
Feeling unusually confident or invincible
Depression started before age 25
Multiple antidepressants haven't worked
Antidepressants caused agitation or 'activation'
Family history of bipolar disorder
Postpartum depression or psychosis
Seasonal pattern (depression in winter, hypomania in spring)

content.text: If antidepressants make you feel worse—agitated, restless, unable to sleep, or 'wired'—this could indicate bipolar disorder. Tell your doctor immediately.
Treating bipolar depression with antidepressants alone can:

items: Trigger mania or hypomania
Cause rapid cycling between moods
Worsen the long-term course
Lead to mixed episodes (depression + manic energy = dangerous)

content.text: Proper treatment (mood stabilizers, sometimes with antidepressants) prevents mood episodes and provides stability.

items: 'Have I ever had a period where I needed less sleep but felt fine?'
'Have I had episodes of unusual productivity or confidence?'
'Have I made impulsive decisions I later regretted (spending, sex, business)?'
'Do my moods cycle—weeks of depression then weeks of feeling great?'
'Did antidepressants ever make me feel weird or activated?'
'Does anyone in my family have bipolar disorder?'
Ask for a mood disorder specialist (psychiatrist preferred)
Bring someone who knows you well to the appointment
Use a mood chart to track patterns
Be honest about 'good' periods, not just bad ones
Request structured diagnostic interview (SCID, MDQ)

content.text: If your depression hasn't responded to treatment, or you've had periods of unusually elevated mood/energy, talk to your doctor about bipolar disorder. Correct diagnosis changes everything—including which medications will actually help.
